newsitem.title: JAPAN: Iraq envoy says hopes oil ban lifted this year.
newsitem.headline: Iraq envoy says hopes oil ban lifted this year.

text.p: Iraq hopes to soon clear away concerns about its weapons programme, paving the way for an end to a U.N.-imposed economic ban and a full return to the world oil market, an Iraqi official said on Friday.

Abdul-Amir al-Anbari, an Iraqi envoy who has led Baghdad's oil-for-food talks with the United Nations, told Reuters in an interview that he hoped to see a global ban on Iraqi oil exports lifted by the end of this year.
He said he believes Iraq will be able to meet the key condition for the sanctions to be removed, that Baghdad fully account for and eliminate weapons of mass destruction.
"We hope by the end of the year to have a clean slate," Anbari said.

Anbari has been in Japan since Monday as part of Baghdad's bid to drum up global support for its long-standing objective to secure the lifting of U.N. economic sanctions imposed since Iraqi troops invaded neighbouring Kuwait in August 1990.
He said that the tide of opinion within the U.N. Security Council was shifting towards lifting the sanctions by the end of this year.
The U.N. Security Council -- meeting as part of its regular 60-day review of sanctions against Iraq -- decided earlier this month to maintain the economic ban imposed against Iraq.

Rolf Ekeus, head of the U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM) which is in charge of ridding Iraq of clandestine weapons, told the council that it was not fully satisfied with Iraq's disclosure of its weapons operations.
The Iraqi envoy maintained, however, that the issue would soon be resolved.
"We believe the missile issue...is behind us now. We believe soon the chemical and biological weapons issue would also be over," Anbari said.
On the oil-for-food deal, Anbari expressed deep dissatisfaction with the pace at which humanitarian aid bought by money from the oil sales was being delivered to Iraq.
The U.N. agreement, implemented in December, allows Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months.
Anbari expressed unhappiness over the ceiling set on the value of oil that could be sold, saying that the amount per person was virtually "nothing".

He said Iraq exported about three million barrels per day of crude oil before the Gulf War, which roughly amounted to about $10 billion to $12 billion in oil revenues a year. Iraq previously spent $3 billion a year for food and medicine alone, Anbari said.
The first food shipments under the agreement arrived on Thursday, more than three months after the pact was put into effect.
The Iraqi envoy accused the United States and Britain of impeding the progress of the shipments of relief goods.

Foreign Ministry officials told Anbari at a meeting on Wednesday that bilateral ties would improve if Iraq returned to the global community by abiding fully with all U.N. Security Council resolutions.
